column1: SECTION C — HIGH-LEVERAGE PRACTICES (Teacher Pedagogy & Training Curriculum Alignment)

column3: Only yes/no or recall questions asked. Close-ended, requiring one-word answers.
column4: Mix of recall and some open-ended questions, but they lack depth. E.g., 'Why is the capital important?' without further exploration.
column5: Purposeful mix including application & analysis questions. Open-ended questions dominate. Wait time given.
column6: Questions span all Bloom's levels (Remember→Create); students generate questions; Socratic questioning evident.
column8:
L0: Pedagogical Practice (5-step lesson plan)
L1: Open-Ended Questions + Think-Pair-Share + Bloom's Taxonomy
L2: Socratic Questioning + Bloom's 3-level question design
column9:
FICO V3 (C1) + TEACH (Checks for Understanding) + OECD (Cognitive Activation) + HOTS Instructional Strategies ('Teacher poses open-ended and thought-provoking questions')

Why: HOTS-aligned questioning is the gateway to deeper learning. TEACH evidence: classrooms with higher-order questions show 2× learning gains.

column3: Repeats same explanation when students don't understand.
column4: Tries a different approach but still teacher-centered.
column5: Uses alternative representations (visual, concrete, analogy). Adjusts teaching to student level.
column6: Diagnoses misconception, re-explains using student's own logic, confirms understanding.
column8:
L0: Content Expertise (CPA Approach)
L1: Diagnosing misconceptions in operations
L2: Teaching comprehension strategies
column9:
FICO V3 (C2) + TEACH (Checks for Understanding) + OECD (Supportive Climate) + HOTS Instructional Strategies ('Scaffolding is used effectively to help students explore complex ideas')

Why: The ability to re-explain separates trained from untrained teachers. Critical in contexts with no remedial support.

column3: No feedback given, or only 'good/bad' evaluations. Generic: 'Good job' or 'Try again.'
column4: Feedback given but generic ('try harder'). Specific but does not consistently guide improvement.
column5: Specific feedback on what was done well and what to improve. Actionable.
column6: Feedback is specific, actionable, with next steps. Students use feedback to self-correct. Guides refinement of reasoning.
column8:
L0: Assessment & Feedback (positive verbal feedback, quick checks)
L1: Formative assessments + data-driven adjustments
L2: Rubrics + self-assessment + peer assessment
column9:
FICO V3 (C3) + TEACH (Feedback) + OECD (Supportive Climate) + HOTS Assessment & Feedback ('Feedback that guides students in refining reasoning or solutions')

Why: Hattie's meta-analysis: feedback has d=0.73 effect size. But only when specific and actionable. HOTS rubric demands reasoning-focused feedback.

column3: Only 2–3 students participate; others ignored. Teacher-dominated.
column4: Teacher calls on volunteers only. A few students contribute while others stay silent.
column5: Deliberate strategies: cold call, pair-share, name sticks. Diverse students included.
column6: All students participate; teacher tracks contributions; gender-equitable. Students debate and refine arguments.
column8:
L0: Inclusive Education (recognizing diverse learners)
L1: Student-centered strategies in overcrowded classrooms + peer teaching
L2: Differentiated instruction + learning stations
column9:
FICO V3 (C4) + TEACH (Culture of Learning) + OECD (Supportive Climate) + HOTS Student Engagement ('Students actively engage in discussions and debates')

Why: In Pakistani classrooms, participation skews male and toward front-row students. HOTS requires ALL students in complex discussions.

column3: Students are passive recipients; no choice or voice. Content from single perspective.
column4: Occasional student input but teacher-dominated. Multiple perspectives mentioned but not explored.
column5: Students make choices about how to demonstrate learning. Explore multiple perspectives.
column6: Students lead discussions, choose methods, self-assess, peer-teach. Create novel solutions. Evaluate alternatives.
column8:
L1: Think-Pair-Share + brainstorming
L2: Student-led discussions + PBL task design + multiple solution approaches
L3: Student-led behavior committees + peer mentoring
column9:
FICO V3 (C5) + OECD (Cognitive Activation) + HOTS Student Engagement ('Students explore multiple perspectives or create novel solutions')

Why: Agency bridges compliance to ownership. HOTS levels of Create and Evaluate require student-initiated thinking.

column3: Frequent disruptions; no visible routines. Students struggle to engage.
column4: Some routines but inconsistently enforced. Instructions lack clarity for all groups.
column5: Clear routines (entry, transitions, dismissal); minimal disruptions. Expectations clear.
column6: Seamless routines; students self-manage; positive behavioral reinforcement. Students actively participate in complex, clearly defined tasks.
column8:
L0: Classroom Management (routines, rules, attention strategies)
L1: SMART goals for behavior + behavior charts
L2: Restorative practices + positive reinforcement + classroom vision
L3: School-wide behavior programs + peer mentoring
column9:
TEACH (Classroom Culture — Behavioral Expectations) + OECD (Classroom Management) + HOTS Classroom Environment ('Students actively encouraged to participate in complex tasks with clear expectations')

Why: TEACH Area 2: Classroom culture is prerequisite for all learning. HOTS rubric ties management directly to complex task engagement.

column3: Negative tone; punitive language or humiliation.
column5: Warm, encouraging tone; mistakes treated as learning opportunities.
column6: Joyful classroom; students feel safe to take risks; laughter and curiosity present.
column8:
L0: Inclusive Education (child psychology fundamentals)
L1: Child psychology application + UDL
L2: Restorative circles + emotional check-ins + advanced psychology
column9:
TEACH (Culture of Learning — Positive Language) + OECD (Supportive Climate) + HOTS Classroom Environment ('Classroom fosters open discussions and critical thinking')

Why: Children who feel psychologically safe learn 2× faster (Durlak et al., 2011). HOTS requires open discussion which demands safety.

column3: Teacher tells but doesn't show. Simple tasks demonstrated without explanation of process.
column4: Teacher demonstrates once but moves on quickly. Problem-solving modeled but strategies not explained.
column5: I Do → We Do → You Do scaffolding visible. Problem-solving and creativity modeled with clear strategies.
column6: Gradual release with checks at each stage; scaffold removed when ready. Teacher brainstorms solutions and explains reasoning.
column8:
L0: Pedagogical Practice (5-step lesson plan + diagrams)
L1: Scaffolding complex concepts + GRR model
L2: Inquiry-based learning + PBL design
column9:
TEACH (Lesson Facilitation — Explicit Teaching) + OECD (Instructional Clarity) + HOTS Instructional Strategies ('Teacher demonstrates problem-solving and creativity in real-time scenarios')

Why: Vygotsky's ZPD in practice. HOTS rubric specifically requires real-time problem-solving demonstration.

column3: No group or pair work. Students work individually without interaction.
column4: Students in groups but working individually. Tasks lack depth.
column5: Purposeful pair/group tasks with clear roles. Students work towards synthesized solutions.
column6: Structured collaboration (think-pair-share, jigsaw); students build on each other's ideas. Teams design solutions to community problems.
column8:
L0: Pedagogical Practice (group reading)
L1: Peer teaching + Think-Pair-Share
L2: Small-group problem-solving + student-led role assignment
L3: PBL showcases + interdisciplinary projects
column9:
OECD (Cognitive Activation — Collaborative Problem Solving) + HOTS Student Engagement ('Students collaborate on tasks requiring synthesis, evaluation, or innovative problem-solving')

Why: HOTS rubric demands collaboration focused on synthesis and problem-solving, not just sitting together.

column5: Taleemabad videos/apps used to support learning objectives.
column6: Technology integrated seamlessly; students interact with content; teacher facilitates around it.
column8:
L0: Digital Literacy (YouTube, Google search, Slides)
L1: Blended learning + Google Forms + digital checklists
L2: Canva + Google Drive + interactive digital resources + Google Meet
L3: School-wide flipped classroom + digital tool workshops
column9:
FICO V3 (Original Fidelity) + Taleemabad Curriculum Design + Training Curriculum (Digital Literacy domain L0–L3)

Why: This is Taleemabad's core value proposition — tech-enhanced teaching. Fidelity to tech integration = fidelity to the model.

column3: Assessment limited to teacher-led grading. Students receive grades without reflection.
column4: Some self- or peer-assessment occurs, but inconsistent. Students assess without clear criteria.
column5: Self- and peer-assessment structured and purposeful. Students use rubrics to assess work.
column6: Students use rubrics to assess work, suggest improvements for peers, and set goals. Assessment tasks require analysis/evaluation/creation.
column8:
L0: Assessment & Feedback (checklists, verbal feedback)
L1: Formative + summative assessments + seen vs unseen questions
L2: Self-assessment + student portfolios + peer review + rubric design
L3: School-wide assessment systems + data dashboards
column9:
HOTS Assessment & Feedback ('Students engage in self-assessment or peer-assessment to evaluate reasoning') + TEACH (Checks for Understanding)

Why: HOTS rubric makes this a standalone indicator. Self/peer assessment builds metacognition — the highest leverage skill.

column3: Resources and space disorganized, limiting collaborative learning. No group work areas.
column4: Some organization, but space/resources do not fully support collaboration.
column5: Resources and space well-organized for collaborative tasks. Materials accessible.
column6: Tables arranged for group work, materials easily accessible. Environment designed for inquiry and collaboration.
column8:
L0: Inclusive Education (visual/auditory aids, differentiated materials)
L1: Scaffolded lessons + learning stations
L2: Assistive technologies + differentiated homework
L3: Community-based inclusive projects
column9:
HOTS Classroom Environment ('Resources and space are organized to support collaboration and problem-solving') + OECD (Active Learning)

Why: HOTS rubric includes physical environment as observable indicator. In Pakistani classrooms, space arrangement directly predicts collaboration quality.
